archetype.name: Improviser (holds the ball)
archetype.definition: A second-year passer who works short, holds the ball past three seconds hunting for something better, and lives on the occasional deep strike, while taking more sacks than almost anyone.

report.headline: Three deep strikes carried a sack-heavy start; the rest still looks like 2025.
report.take:
Shedeur Sanders is Cleveland's backup who got one real start this year. With Deshaun Watson out with a concussion, he played every snap in Week 9 at New Orleans and went 19 of 31 for 297 yards, two touchdowns, no interceptions and five sacks in a one-point loss. On the surface that is a breakout: 9.58 yards per attempt and 10.39 adjusted net yards per dropback as a starter, with his season ANY/A ranked 2nd of 49. Against last year's rookie tape (56.6% completions, 6.6 YPA, 10 interceptions in eight games, -0.188 EPA per play ranked 55th of 63), it looks like a different quarterback.

The depth splits tell a narrower story. His three throws of 20-plus air yards all connected and added 11.1 EPA. Everything else was underwater: throws under 10 air yards came to -1.3 EPA in total, screens and throws behind the line to -4.9, he went 0 for 4 on intermediate throws, and his five red-zone plays cost -4.9. Count the sacks and scrambles and his 46 dropbacks added up to -1.8 EPA. Three completions are carrying the line. His completion rate over expected is -6.71, 43rd of 49, and his intended air yards sit 2.63 short of the sticks. This is a conservative short game that doesn't win on its own, plus a few big shots.

The sacks are the thread from last year. He held the ball 3.09 seconds (3.23 as a rookie), scrambled on 15.2% of dropbacks for little gain, and was sacked on 12.8% of them, 48th of 49. Cleveland's line allows the highest hit rate in the league, so part of this is the protection. But a quarterback who holds it that long behind that line will keep taking sacks; it comes with how he plays. The zero interceptions on 34 attempts is a welcome change from last year's one-plus a game, but it is too few throws to call a fix. The charted pressure and bad-throw numbers also look incomplete, so I'm not leaning on them.

Where it goes depends on whether Watson is back. If Sanders keeps starting, expect yardage that depends on explosive plays, sack totals that stall drives, and real week-to-week swings. The deep hits show the arm and the willingness to throw downfield. The short game and his sack rate will decide whether that is enough.

strengths.title: Hits the deep shots he takes
strengths.body: All three of his 20-plus-air-yard throws connected, and those plays added more EPA than the rest of his passing combined. It shows he will throw downfield into tight windows and can place the ball when he does. Three attempts is a hint, not a rate: the share of deep shots that land will come down. The willingness should carry over, though, and it gives the offense a way to score that it otherwise lacks.

strengths.title: Ball security, so far
strengths.body: He has no interceptions and no lost fumbles this season. After 10 interceptions in eight games as a rookie, that is the most meaningful change in his profile if it holds. He has kept the ball out of harm's way partly by throwing short and taking sacks instead of forcing throws, which is a cost of its own. On 34 attempts, treat it as an encouraging sign rather than a settled trait.

strengths.title: Connection with KC Concepcion
strengths.body: Concepcion turned six targets into more than a point of EPA per target, the best rate of anyone he threw to. Denzel Boston drew the most volume and was productive too. A young quarterback needs a reliable receiver who wins downfield, and this is the pairing to watch.

concerns.title: Sacks that kill drives
concerns.body: His sack rate is second-worst among 49 qualifiers, and it was 13.9% in his lone start. Cleveland's line allows the league's highest hit rate, so the protection is part of it. So is his own play: a 3.09-second time to throw and frequent scrambles that rarely gain much. Unless he speeds up his reads, this lasts as long as he starts.

concerns.title: Short game isn't moving the ball
concerns.body: Throws under 10 air yards were net negative, screens and throws behind the line were worse, and he missed all four intermediate throws. For a passer throwing short of the sticks this often, the routine completions have to pay off, and they haven't. His completion rate over expected sits near the bottom of the league, as it did last year, so his accuracy looks like a lasting problem rather than a slump.

concerns.title: Red-zone stalls
concerns.body: His five red-zone plays all failed and cost nearly five points of EPA, two of them sacks. When the field shrinks, the deep shots disappear and the long hold gets punished. It is a small sample, but it fits the rest of his profile.

trend.note: He played mop-up snaps in Weeks 3 and 8, then a full, explosive but sack-strewn start in Week 9. One start is all there is, and it was efficient by yards per attempt but negative once sacks and the short game are counted.

nextGame.headline: Houston's pass rush meets his sacks, but its secondary leaks big plays
nextGame.body:
Houston is the sharpest version of his own trade-off. Its defense has the league's second-best sack rate and the seventh-best hit rate, against a Cleveland line that allows the most hits in football and a quarterback who holds the ball over three seconds. That points to more sacks and stalled drives. Houston also allows the highest rate of explosive passes in the league and ranks 24th in EPA allowed on deep throws, exactly where his start was won. Offenses pass on Houston more than usual, and its pass defense overall is middling at 18th. The Book has Cleveland as a 4.5-point home underdog with a low 39.5 total, which reads as a grind with a few chances for big plays.

Availability drives this one. Watson is listed out with the concussion, though his estimated return date falls on game day and the depth chart still had Sanders at QB2 as of November 10, so the start is likely but not locked. On Houston's side, safety Reed Blankenship (86% of snaps) is out, which removes a regular from the back end against a quarterback whose best plays came deep. Running back David Montgomery is also out, thinning a Houston run game that already ranks 25th. That could lean Houston toward passing and a quicker game, which would push Cleveland to throw more.

keyMatchups.title: Houston rush versus the long hold
keyMatchups.body: Houston gets home on 9.2% of dropbacks, second in the league, and Sanders has been sacked on 12.8% of his. If he holds the ball the way he did in New Orleans, this matchup decides the game. Quicker throws would help, but his short game hasn't produced.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots at a leaky secondary
keyMatchups.body: Houston gives up the league's highest explosive-pass rate and plays without its starting safety. That fits the one part of his game that has worked. If he gets even two clean deep looks, the yardage can come quickly.

keyMatchups.title: The No. 2 receiver's opening
keyMatchups.body: Houston's defense lets a team's second receiver score well above his usual level, one of the worst marks in the league, while it holds top tight ends down. That favors spreading the ball to Boston and Concepcion rather than working the tight end.

nextGame.watch: His sack count. If Houston keeps him to two or three while the deep shots keep landing, his first start was more than a fluke; four or more means the pressure problem is winning.

restOfSeason.body: Everything hinges on Watson's concussion recovery. When Watson returns, Sanders goes back to the bench and his numbers stop. While he starts, expect him to keep pushing the ball downfield and to keep taking a lot of sacks behind this line. The near-perfect deep efficiency will come down, and so will the 9-plus yards per attempt. The near-bottom completion rate over expected and the long time to throw have held up across both seasons and look like who he is. As a starter I'd project roughly 185-260 passing yards and about one touchdown a game, with three to five sacks. The zero interceptions should give way to an occasional pick, though fewer than last year's rate if he keeps protecting the ball.

confidence.note: One start, 34 attempts on the season, and his job depends on Watson's concussion timeline.
